q: Both B and T lymphocytes arise from stem cells located in the:
x: All lymphocytes are produced from stem cells in the red bone marrow. They then mature in different places: B cells in the bone marrow and T cells in the thymus.

q: T lymphocytes complete their maturation in the:
x: Immature lymphocytes that travel to the thymus mature there into T cells; the letter T stands for thymus. B cells mature in the bone marrow.

q: In humans, B lymphocytes become mature and immunocompetent in the:
x: In humans B cells both arise and mature in the bone marrow. Lymph nodes and tonsils are where mature lymphocytes meet antigens, not where B cells mature; the thymus matures T cells.

q: B lymphocytes were first shown to mature in a special organ of birds. This organ is the:
x: In birds B cells mature in the bursa of Fabricius, which gave B cells their name. In mammals the bone marrow does this job. The thymus matures T cells in both groups.

q: Humoral (antibody-mediated) immunity is the function of:
x: B lymphocytes give rise to plasma cells that release antibodies into blood and lymph (the body fluids or 'humours'). Cytotoxic T cells give cell-mediated immunity; neutrophils and macrophages are non-specific phagocytes.

q: Cell-mediated immunity is carried out mainly by:
x: In cell-mediated immunity T lymphocytes act directly against infected, cancerous or foreign cells instead of releasing antibodies. Plasma cells and memory B cells belong to the humoral (B cell) response.

q: The cells that secrete large amounts of antibodies are:
x: When a B cell is activated by its antigen it divides and many daughter cells become plasma cells, which secrete antibodies at a high rate. Memory B cells do not secrete antibodies; they wait for a later exposure.

q: An antigen binds only to the few B cells whose receptors fit it, and these cells then divide to form a large group of identical cells. This is called:
x: In clonal selection the antigen 'selects' the lymphocytes with matching receptors, which then multiply into a clone of identical cells. Diapedesis is the squeezing of white cells out through capillary walls.

q: Memory cells formed during the first exposure to an antigen are responsible for:
o: The faster and stronger response on a later exposure
Immediate inflammation at the site of a wound
Production of interferon by infected cells
The rise in body temperature during fever
x: Memory cells survive long after an infection and recognise the same antigen quickly next time, giving a faster, larger secondary response. Inflammation, interferon and fever are non-specific defences.

q: Which type of T cell directly destroys body cells infected with a virus?
x: Cytotoxic T cells recognise antigen displayed on infected cells and kill those cells. Helper T cells activate other lymphocytes, and suppressor T cells slow the response down; neither kills the cell itself.

q: Helper T cells take part in the immune response mainly by:
o: Secreting chemicals that activate B cells and other T cells
x: Helper T cells release chemical messengers (lymphokines or cytokines) that stimulate B cells to form plasma cells and activate cytotoxic T cells. They do not secrete antibodies or kill cells themselves.

q: The role of suppressor T cells is to:
o: Remember an antigen for many years
Turn down the immune response once the infection is controlled
x: Suppressor T cells inhibit B and T cell activity, so the response switches off when it is no longer needed. Killing cancer cells is done by cytotoxic T cells and antibody production by plasma cells.

q: HIV weakens the immune system mainly by infecting and destroying:
x: HIV attacks helper T cells. As their number falls, both antibody and cell-mediated responses fail and the person becomes open to infections, which leads to AIDS.

q: A patient's helper T cell count falls to a very low level. Which effect on the immune system is expected?
o: Only the skin and mucous barriers stop working
Antibody production rises to make up for the loss
Only cell-mediated immunity is affected, antibodies stay normal
Both antibody production and cytotoxic T cell activity are reduced
x: Helper T cells activate both B cells (for antibodies) and cytotoxic T cells, so losing them weakens both arms of specific immunity. Skin and mucous barriers are non-specific and do not depend on T cells.

q: Rejection of a transplanted kidney from an unmatched donor is mainly due to:
o: IgE antibodies binding to mast cells
Interferon released by the new kidney
Lack of red blood cells in the graft
Cytotoxic T cells attacking the foreign cells
x: The donor's cells carry surface antigens that the recipient recognises as non-self, and cytotoxic T cells attack them. This is why tissues are matched and drugs that suppress the immune system are given.

q: Antibodies are chemically:
x: Antibodies are proteins called immunoglobulins (they are in the gamma globulin part of plasma proteins). Their protein structure lets them fold into exact shapes that fit antigens.

q: A single Y-shaped antibody molecule is made of:
o: Two heavy and two light polypeptide chains
One heavy and one light polypeptide chain
x: The basic antibody unit has four polypeptide chains: two identical heavy chains and two identical light chains, arranged in a Y shape.

q: The four polypeptide chains of an antibody are held together by:
x: Disulfide (S–S) bridges link the heavy chains to each other and each light chain to a heavy chain. Glycosidic bonds join sugars and phosphodiester bonds join nucleotides.

q: The antigen-binding sites of an antibody are located in the:
o: Variable regions at the tips of the arms
x: The tips of the two arms are variable regions whose amino acid sequence differs from antibody to antibody, giving each a shape that fits one antigen. The constant region is the same within a class.

q: How many antigen-binding sites does one IgG molecule have?
x: IgG is a single Y-shaped unit with one binding site at the tip of each arm, so it has two. Pentameric IgM, by contrast, has ten.

q: The body can make antibodies against a huge range of different antigens. The specificity of each antibody depends on:
o: The number of heavy chains it has
The amino acid sequence of its variable regions
The number of disulfide bonds in its stem
x: Different amino acid sequences in the variable regions give binding sites of different shapes, each fitting a particular antigen. All antibodies have two heavy chains, and the constant region decides the class, not the antigen it binds.

q: Which class of antibody can cross the placenta from mother to fetus?
x: IgG is the only antibody class that crosses the placenta, giving the newborn passive protection. IgM is too large to cross, and IgA reaches the baby later through breast milk.

q: The most abundant class of antibody in human blood plasma is:
x: IgG makes up most (about three quarters) of the antibodies in plasma. IgE and IgD are present only in very small amounts.

q: Which antibody is a pentamer and is the first class produced in a primary immune response?
x: IgM is made of five Y-shaped units joined together and is the first antibody to appear after a first exposure. IgG takes over later and dominates the secondary response.

q: The antibody class found mainly in secretions such as tears, saliva and breast milk is:
x: IgA, often as a dimer, is secreted onto mucous surfaces and into tears, saliva and milk, protecting the entry points of the body. IgE is linked with allergy.

q: Which antibody class binds to mast cells and is involved in allergic reactions?
x: IgE attaches to mast cells; when the allergen binds, the mast cells release histamine, causing allergy symptoms. IgE is also involved in defence against parasitic worms.

q: Which antibody class is found mainly as an antigen receptor on the surface of B cells and is present in only tiny amounts in plasma?
x: IgD occurs mostly on the B cell surface, where it acts as a receptor for antigen; very little circulates. IgG, IgA and IgM are all present in plasma in large amounts.

q: How many classes of antibodies (immunoglobulins) are found in humans?
x: There are five classes: IgG, IgA, IgM, IgD and IgE. They differ in the constant region of their heavy chains.

q: An antigen is:
o: Any molecule recognised as foreign that triggers an immune response
A protein made by plasma cells that destroys germs
A white blood cell that engulfs bacteria
A chemical made by infected cells to protect neighbouring cells
x: An antigen is a molecule, usually a protein or polysaccharide on a pathogen or foreign cell, that the body recognises as non-self and that stimulates antibody or T cell responses. A protein made by plasma cells is an antibody, and a protective chemical from infected cells describes interferon.

q: The specific part of an antigen molecule to which an antibody binds is called the:
x: An antibody recognises a small region on the antigen called the antigenic determinant (epitope). Variable, constant and hinge regions are parts of the antibody, not the antigen.

q: Antibodies link many bacterial cells together into clumps. This reaction is called:
x: Because each antibody has at least two binding sites, it can bridge antigens on different cells and clump them together: agglutination. Precipitation applies to soluble antigens, which form an insoluble complex.

q: When antibodies combine with soluble antigens and form insoluble complexes that settle out, the reaction is:
x: Precipitation turns dissolved antigens into insoluble antigen–antibody complexes that phagocytes can remove. Agglutination is the clumping of whole cells.

q: Antibodies against tetanus toxin bind to the toxin and block its harmful action. This is an example of:
x: In neutralisation antibodies cover the active sites of toxins, or the attachment sites of viruses, so they can no longer harm cells. No cells are clumped or burst.

q: Antibodies bound to the surface of a bacterial cell can lead to holes being made in its membrane so that it bursts. This happens through activation of:
x: Antibody bound to a cell can activate complement, a group of plasma proteins that punch holes in the cell membrane and cause lysis. Interferon protects cells against viruses and histamine is released in inflammation and allergy.

q: How does agglutination of bacteria by antibodies help the body get rid of them?
o: The clumps release toxins that kill other bacteria
Agglutination converts bacteria into memory cells
The clumps are easily engulfed and destroyed by phagocytes
The clumps are dissolved directly by the antibodies
x: Clumped bacteria cannot spread easily and are readily ingested by phagocytes such as macrophages and neutrophils. Antibodies themselves do not digest bacteria.

q: Compared with the secondary immune response, the primary immune response is:
o: Equally fast but produces more antibody
Faster but lasts for a shorter time
x: On first exposure there are few lymphocytes that match the antigen, so antibodies appear after a lag and reach a low level. On second exposure memory cells give a faster, larger and longer-lasting response.

q: The antibody class that forms most of the antibody produced in a secondary immune response is:
x: IgM appears first in a primary response, but in the secondary response memory cells quickly produce large amounts of IgG, which therefore dominates.

q: Why is there a lag of several days before antibodies appear in a primary immune response?
o: Antibodies must first be absorbed from the gut
The antigen must first be destroyed by the liver
Only a few matching lymphocytes exist and they must first divide and differentiate
Plasma cells must first travel to the thymus to mature
x: Before the first exposure only a small number of lymphocytes fit the antigen. These must be selected, multiply into a clone and become plasma cells before much antibody is made, which takes time.

q: The immunity a person develops after recovering from chickenpox is:
x: The person's own immune system made antibodies and memory cells (active) in response to a natural infection (natural). Vaccination would make it artificial.

q: Immunity produced by a vaccine against measles is:
x: The vaccine is given deliberately (artificial), and the body makes its own antibodies and memory cells against it (active).

q: A newborn baby is protected for a few months by antibodies that crossed the placenta from its mother. This is:
x: The baby receives ready-made antibodies (passive) by a normal body process (natural). Because the baby did not make them, no memory cells form and the protection fades.

q: A person bitten by a snake is injected with antivenom serum containing ready-made antibodies. The immunity given is:
x: Ready-made antibodies from another source are given by injection, so the immunity is passive and artificial. The person's own lymphocytes are not stimulated to make antibodies.

q: The main advantage of passive immunity over active immunity is that it:
o: Lasts for the whole of life
Produces large numbers of memory cells
Makes the person's own plasma cells active
x: Passive immunity gives ready-made antibodies, so protection starts at once. It is short-lived and forms no memory cells; active immunity takes time to develop but lasts much longer.

q: Why does passive immunity last only a few weeks or months?
o: The received antibodies are broken down and no memory cells are formed
The antibodies received stimulate suppressor T cells
The antibodies are excreted at once by the kidneys
Passive antibodies only bind to self antigens
x: The donated antibodies are gradually broken down, and because the person's own lymphocytes were not stimulated, no memory cells exist to make more. So protection fades.

q: Which statement about breast-feeding and immunity is correct?
o: Breast milk gives the baby artificial passive immunity
Breast milk contains memory T cells that settle in the baby's thymus
Breast milk supplies IgA antibodies, giving natural passive immunity
Breast milk gives the baby active immunity against all diseases
x: Mother's milk, especially colostrum, contains IgA antibodies that protect the baby's gut. Ready-made antibodies received naturally give natural passive immunity.

q: Active immunity usually lasts much longer than passive immunity because:
o: Antibodies in active immunity are never broken down
Memory cells are formed in active immunity
Active immunity uses only non-specific defences
x: In active immunity the body's own lymphocytes respond and leave long-lived memory cells that can quickly produce antibody again. Antibodies themselves are broken down in both cases.

q: Which of the following is NOT used as a vaccine?
o: Antibodies taken from an immunised horse
x: Antibodies from an immunised animal form an antiserum, which gives passive immunity and is not a vaccine. Vaccines contain antigens (killed or weakened microbes, toxoids or their parts) that make the body build its own active immunity.

q: Vaccines against tetanus and diphtheria contain toxoids. A toxoid is:
o: A live, weakened form of the bacterium
A bacterial toxin treated so it is harmless but still antigenic
An antibody that neutralises the toxin
A drug that kills the bacterium
x: A toxoid is a toxin made harmless (for example by chemical treatment) that still has its antigenic shape, so the body makes antibodies and memory cells against the real toxin.

q: Edward Jenner developed the first vaccine, using material from cowpox, to protect against:
x: In 1796 Jenner used cowpox material to protect people against the related smallpox virus. Rabies vaccine was later developed by Louis Pasteur.

q: Booster doses of a vaccine are given some time after the first dose because they:
o: Trigger a secondary response, raising antibody levels and memory cells
Destroy memory cells formed by the first dose
Replace the need for active immunity
x: The first dose produces a primary response and memory cells. A booster re-exposes the body to the antigen, giving a quicker, larger secondary response and stronger, longer-lasting immunity.

q: The oral (Sabin) polio vaccine contains:
x: Sabin's oral vaccine uses live but weakened poliovirus that multiplies harmlessly and stimulates immunity. Polio is a viral disease and has no toxoid; Salk's injected vaccine uses killed virus.

q: Which statement about B and T lymphocytes is correct?
o: B cells release antibodies that act at a distance; T cells act on cells directly
T cells secrete antibodies, while B cells kill infected cells
B cells mature in the thymus, while T cells mature in the bone marrow
Both types are produced only after an infection begins
x: B cells give rise to plasma cells whose antibodies circulate in body fluids, while T cells must contact the target cells. B cells mature in the bone marrow and T cells in the thymus, and both exist before any infection.

q: Which of the following is part of the specific defence of the body?
x: Antibodies are made against one particular antigen, so they are a specific defence. Stomach acid, skin and inflammation act the same way against any invader and are non-specific.

q: The two features that distinguish specific immunity from non-specific defence are:
o: Speed of action and use of phagocytes
Recognition of particular antigens and memory
x: Specific immunity targets particular antigens and remembers them, so later responses are faster. Phagocytes, fever, histamine and barriers are parts of non-specific defence.

q: Which is NOT a feature of the specific immune response?
o: It is directed at particular antigens
It acts in the same way against every kind of pathogen
x: Acting in the same way against every pathogen describes non-specific defence such as skin or phagocytes. Specific immunity is targeted, has memory and normally ignores self.

q: When the immune system fails to recognise the body's own cells as self and attacks them, the condition is called:
x: Normally lymphocytes tolerate self antigens. In autoimmune disease this tolerance fails and the body attacks its own tissues. Allergy is an over-reaction to a harmless foreign substance.

q: In an allergic reaction to pollen, the histamine that causes sneezing and swelling is released from:
x: IgE antibodies sit on mast cells; when pollen (the allergen) binds to them, the mast cells release histamine. Plasma cells make the IgE but do not release histamine.

q: What is the correct order of events in the humoral immune response?
o: Antigen recognition by B cell → clone formation → plasma cells form → antibody secretion
Antibody secretion → antigen recognition → clone formation → plasma cell formation
Plasma cell formation → antigen recognition → clone formation → antibody secretion
Clone formation → antibody secretion → antigen recognition → plasma cell formation
x: A B cell first binds its specific antigen, then divides into a clone; most clone cells become plasma cells (others memory cells), and the plasma cells secrete antibodies.

q: The thymus is most active and relatively largest in a human:
x: The thymus is large and active in childhood, when most T cells are being matured, and it shrinks after puberty. Mature T cells then persist in lymph nodes and blood.

q: Macrophages help the specific immune response by:
o: Maturing T cells in the thymus
Engulfing pathogens and displaying their antigens to helper T cells
x: Macrophages are antigen-presenting cells: they ingest a pathogen and display pieces of its antigens on their surface, which activates helper T cells. They do not make antibodies.

q: A person who had measles as a child never gets it again, yet catches influenza almost every year. The best explanation is that:
o: Influenza virus destroys all memory cells
Measles memory cells also destroy influenza virus
Influenza is a bacterial disease and cannot be remembered
Influenza virus frequently changes its surface antigens, so old memory cells do not match
x: Memory cells recognise one antigen shape. Measles virus stays antigenically stable, but influenza virus keeps changing its surface antigens, so each new strain meets an unprimed immune system. Influenza is a viral disease.

q: In the plasma proteins, antibodies belong to the fraction called:
x: Antibodies (immunoglobulins) are gamma globulins. Albumins mainly maintain osmotic pressure, and fibrinogen takes part in blood clotting.

q: A person who was never vaccinated against tetanus gets a deep, dirty wound. The doctor gives anti-tetanus serum (antitoxin) as well as toxoid. The antitoxin is needed because:
o: It stimulates the formation of memory cells
It gives ready-made antibodies at once, while the toxoid takes days to act
It kills the tetanus bacteria directly like an antibiotic
It prevents the toxoid from causing disease
x: The toxoid produces active immunity, but this takes days to develop. The antitoxin supplies ready-made antibodies (artificial passive immunity) that neutralise the toxin immediately; it forms no memory cells.

q: The hinge region of an antibody molecule allows the antibody to:
o: Change from one class to another
Move its arms so it can bind antigens at different distances apart
x: The hinge region, where the arms join the stem, is flexible, so the two binding arms can open or close to fit antigenic determinants spaced at different distances.

q: The class of an antibody (IgG, IgA, IgM, IgD or IgE) is determined by:
o: The variable region of its light chains
The constant region of its heavy chains
The number of disulfide bonds in its arms
x: The constant region of the heavy chains differs between the five classes and decides how the antibody behaves, for example crossing the placenta. The variable region decides which antigen is bound.
